title: FAQ sections that help buyers and search engines
metaTitle: FAQ page SEO that helps real buyers
excerpt: FAQ sections earn their place when they answer questions buyers already ask, in text those buyers can read. Markup should describe that same visible text.
alt: Hands typing on a laptop at a wooden desk near a window, the quiet work of writing answers a buyer could actually use.
caption: Writing answers at a wooden desk, where the questions have to be ones a buyer would ask. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How many questions belong on a homepage FAQ?
faqs.answer: Four to six is enough for a small company site. Cover the doubts that stall a decision, such as timeline, what to prepare, what the client owns, how revisions work, and whether the same team designs and builds. Add a question when real conversations repeat it, and remove one nobody asks.

faqs.question: When should FAQ schema be added?
faqs.answer: Add it after the questions and answers are visible on the page, and keep the markup the same as that text. Schema.org's FAQPage type describes a page that presents frequently asked questions, so hidden questions do not qualify. If the writing is not on the page yet, leave the markup off.

faqs.question: Should every blog post have an FAQ?
faqs.answer: A post can end with three questions a reader would still have after the article. Each answer should stand on its own in a few sentences. Skip the block when you would only be repeating the headings.

markdown:
FAQ page SEO works when a buyer uses the block to settle a doubt before they write to you. Search uses the same block when the wording matches how people ask. Both jobs fail when the questions are invented for a crawler, or when the answers exist only in a script the visitor never sees.

Keep the list short. Collect the questions founders already ask on calls and in email. Answer them in public, on the page, in the words you would use live. Add FAQ markup only for that visible text.

## Questions a buyer actually has

Start from the inbox, not from a keyword tool. The useful questions are the ones that stall a decision. On a studio site those are usually about time, readiness, ownership, revisions, and whether the same people design and build. On a product site they are about the job the software does, what happens to the customer's data, and how to undo a mistake. On a shop they are about shipping, returns, and whether a size is in stock.

If you cannot picture a specific person asking the question, leave it off the page. "What makes your solutions innovative?" is a prompt. "Will we own the repository when the project ends?" is a buyer.

[Google's guidance on helpful content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether a reader leaves knowing enough to reach a goal. An FAQ that restates the headline in question form does not do that. An FAQ that removes one real objection does. The test is ordinary: would you be willing to send this answer to a founder who asked the question in a thread, without rewriting it first?

Write the question the way the buyer says it. "Do you design and build, or only one of those?" is a sentence a person uses. "What is your end-to-end capability model?" is a sentence a brochure uses. The first one belongs on the page. The second one can be translated, or dropped.

Keep a running list from real conversations. After a few intro calls, the same three doubts tend to repeat. Those three are the start of the FAQ. Everything else is optional until someone actually asks it.

## Answers that stand alone

Each answer should make sense if it is lifted out of the page. Two to four sentences is enough. State what you do, then the condition that changes it.

A timeline answer can say that a marketing site is scoped from a list of pages and states, and that a date holds when a new page is treated as a change to that list. It should name the shape of the work. It should not stop at "it depends," and it should not promise a day count the studio cannot keep.

Match the voice of the rest of the site. If the homepage is quiet and specific, the FAQ should stay quiet and specific. Hanabi's standard is clarity over complexity, with plain communication and a process that can change. An FAQ is an easy place to check that standard. Short sentences. Concrete nouns. No fog about "synergy" or "digital transformation."

Visible means a person can read it. An accordion is fine when the text is in the page and a click reveals it. A block that exists only inside JSON-LD, or only in a design file, is not an FAQ on the site. [Schema.org](https://schema.org/FAQPage) defines an FAQPage as a web page that presents one or more frequently asked questions. The type describes the page's content. It does not create that content.

Write the answer so a stranger can act on it. "You will own the repository, the domain, and the content logins" is an answer. "Ownership is handled according to the agreement" is a delay. If a legal detail truly varies, say what is typical and where the exception is written.

## Markup after the writing

FAQ markup is a description of content. On Schema.org, an FAQPage is a kind of web page, and the questions are what that page is about. The structured data should name the same questions and answers a visitor can read.

Use the markup when three things are true:

- The questions are ones your buyers ask.
- The answers are in the HTML a person can open.
- You will keep the visible text and the markup in step when either one changes.

Skip the markup when the block is a list of keywords, when the answers are hidden from people, or when a heading happens to end in a question mark. A mismatch describes a different page than the one you published. Leaving the markup off is the cleaner choice until the writing is real.

Hanabi's article pages show FAQs but emit article and breadcrumb schema, not FAQ schema. Google retired FAQ rich results, so the visible answers matter more than adding that markup. The questions are on the page, so the description is allowed to mention them. A homepage FAQ follows the same rule. Write four to six questions out in full. Add the markup afterward, if you want it.

Check the pairing before launch. Read the visible question, then the question in the data. They should be the same sentence. A shortened markup version and a longer visible version will drift the first time someone edits one of them.

## How many questions

A small site needs a small FAQ. Four to six questions on a homepage can cover timeline, what the client should have ready, what they own, how revisions work, and whether the studio writes and builds. A service page carries the questions that belong to that service. A blog post can carry three questions a reader would still have after the article.

Past that, people stop scanning. You also start answering things the page already said, and the FAQ starts to feel like padding. When a question needs a whole article, give the short answer and link to the article. The FAQ stays the version someone can use in a minute.

Review the list a couple of times a year, or after several calls repeat a new doubt. Add that doubt. Remove a question nobody asks. A tool can suggest phrases. A person still decides which ones are real.

Order the questions by the decision, not by the keyword. The doubt that blocks a conversation comes first. A curious side question can sit at the end, or wait for a post.

## Where the block sits

Put the questions where the doubt shows up. On a homepage, that is after the work and the process, and before the last invitation to talk. On a long article, the questions come after the argument, to catch what the piece did not cover. On a product page, they sit near the decision, after the price and the reason the thing exists.

The heading can say "Questions" or "FAQ." Either works when the questions themselves are plain. The heading is a poor place to stack search phrases. The questions do the work.

Treat the FAQ as part of the page's promise. The offer, the proof, and the way to start a conversation still have to be clear around it. [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services) are split so a founder can see design, development, and brand as separate jobs, and the questions on a page should be just as easy to point at.

When the answers are strong enough to be quoted on their own, the next piece is about [writing pages that AI search can cite](/blog/pages-ai-search-can-cite). A visible FAQ is one of the passages those systems can lift. That only helps when the answer was true, specific, and complete before anyone marked it up.
